details: RBMK-1000 primary coolant circuit: two independent loops; each loop: 8 main circulation pumps (MCP; 2-speed motors; 5000 kW each); 4 operating + 4 standby per loop; steam-water drum separators (2 per loop; 8000 kg steam/hr capacity); individual pressure channels (1661 channels total; each 9m active length; 88mm ID Zr-Nb alloy); feed water: demineralized; no boric acid (unlike PWR); coolant enters channel at 270°C; exits at 284-290°C (bulk) with steam quality ~14-19% (two-phase mixture); operating pressure: 7 MPa (70 bar); RBMK absence of boron: deliberate design (void coefficient intended to use steam void fraction for control instead of boric acid); RBMK relies on graphite moderator separate from coolant → allows different coolant physics from PWR
chernobyl_application: RBMK coolant chemistry vs PWR: PWR uses boric acid (H₃BO₃; 1000-2000 ppm at BOC; decreases to 0 at EOC) + lithium hydroxide (pH control); RBMK uses NO boric acid; this is fundamental safety difference; in PWR: boron = backup shutdown + soluble poison; in RBMK: only solid control rods; no boron backup; consequence: when RBMK control rods insufficient (ORM=8 on April 26; accident precondition), NO secondary neutron absorber available; boron-free coolant = positive void coefficient contribution unmitigated; post-1986 modification: no boron added (design too different); instead: increased ORM minimum + shorter rod insertion time
source: Knief 1992 Nuclear Engineering; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; rbmk_core_neutron_physics_REAL.csv; rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv

details: Nitrogen-16 (N-16) production: O-16(n,p)N-16; cross-section = 50 mb at 14 MeV (threshold reaction; fast neutrons only); threshold energy: 9.6 MeV; N-16 t½ = 7.13 seconds; decay: ⁿ¹⁶N → ¹⁶O + β⁻ + ν̄; primary beta: 10.4 MeV (28%); gamma: 6.129 MeV (67%) + 7.115 MeV (5%); N-16 is the primary short-range radiation hazard in operating reactor primary circuit; equilibrium N-16 activity in RBMK coolant: ~10¹⁴ Bq (10⁵ TBq) during operation; decay 10× for each 23.7 seconds (10 half-lives); RBMK steam/water: N-16 in steam phase → turbine hall = radiation hazard during operation; turbine hall dose rate during full power: 10-100 mSv/hr (N-16 dominated); reason turbine hall staff must exit during high-power operation
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl relevance: N-16 hazard moot after accident (reactor shut down; no coolant flow; N-16 fully decayed within 3 minutes of shutdown); N-16 is primary reason PWR and BWR turbines/steam systems require regular maintenance shutdown (N-16 in steam → activation of turbine steel components → Co-58/Co-60 → long-term radiation source); BWR turbine maintenance: primary occupational dose source in nuclear industry; RBMK turbine: direct cycle (steam from reactor → turbine; same as BWR) → N-16 in turbine during operation; why turbine hall workers evacuated rapidly (Dyatlov's order to restart turbine made workers enter active N-16 zone)

details: Water radiolysis in reactor coolant: gamma radiation + neutron bombardment → ionization → radical formation; primary products: OH• (hydroxyl radical), H• (hydrogen radical), e_aq (hydrated electron); secondary products: H₂, O₂, H₂O₂; G-values (molecules per 100 eV): G(H₂)=0.45; G(H₂O₂)=0.72; G(O₂)=0.0 (near zero in neutral water); net reaction at high dose rate: H₂O → H₂ + ½O₂; H₂ generation rate in RBMK: ~1-5 kg/day during full power operation; O₂: oxidizes fuel cladding (zirconium oxide formation); H₂O₂: strong oxidizer → accelerates corrosion; BWR/RBMK: hydrogen injection (HWC = hydrogen water chemistry): addition of H₂ (2-5 ppb) suppresses radiolytic O₂ (recombination: O₂ + H₂ → H₂O with catalyst) → reduces stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in stainless steel components
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl accident H₂ generation: Zr-water reaction above 900°C: Zr + 2H₂O → ZrO₂ + 2H₂ (ΔH = -602 kJ/mol); at 1650°C+ reactor temperature post-accident: massive H₂ generation (estimated 50-100 kg in minutes); H₂ mixed with air → explosive mixture; second explosion April 26 01:23:44: debate whether steam explosion or hydrogen detonation (or both); current scientific consensus (Kholosha 1997; Schentler 2001): FIRST explosion = prompt critical power excursion (steam); SECOND explosion = hydrogen detonation (H₂/air/steam mixture); see rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv for H₂ Zr reaction energy
source: Zinkle 2013 Acta Materialia; Elliot 1994 AECL Report; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; chernobyl_accident_chronology_REAL.csv

details: Zirconium alloy cladding chemistry: RBMK uses Zr-1%Nb alloy (Е110); PWR uses Zircaloy-4 (Zr-1.5Sn-0.2Fe-0.1Cr); all Zr alloys oxidize in water: Zr + 2H₂O → ZrO₂ + 2H₂ (at low T; slow); oxide layer provides protection; growth rate: 1-3 µm/month at 300-320°C; typical oxide thickness at end-of-life: 30-100 µm; pellet-cladding interaction (PCI): thermal cycling causes UO₂ pellet expansion → cladding stress → crack initiation; SCC (stress corrosion cracking): aggressive chemistry (iodine from fission, Cs, Te) + stress → intergranular SCC; iodine primary PCI agent: I₂ formed from I-131 decay → penetrates grain boundaries → brittle fracture; mitigated by: ramping restrictions (avoid rapid power increases); low-tin alloys; soft cladding (AREVA duplex)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl fuel failure: cladding failed before explosion due to: (1) thermal pulse from power excursion 200→30,000 MWt in <4s; (2) cladding temperature >900°C in 4s; (3) Zr-water reaction began immediately; cladding failure = primary fuel dispersal mechanism; intact cladding = barrier 1; failed cladding = all volatile fission products (Cs; I; Te; Xe; Kr) release to coolant and then atmosphere; RBMK channel design (individual pressure tubes vs PWR pressure vessel): means channel failure = local; but 1661 channels = 1661 failure points; in accident: all channels in affected zone failed approximately simultaneously due to excursion
source: Hillner 2000 J Nucl Mater; Garzarolli 2010; rbmk_fuel_specifications_REAL.csv; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; fission_product_yields_REAL.csv

details: Activated corrosion products (ACPs) in reactor cooling circuits: metals corrode from primary circuit stainless steel/Inconel → released as ions/particles into coolant → activated in reactor flux → deposited on out-of-core surfaces = 'shine'; key ACPs: Co-58 (Ni-58 + n → Co-58; t½=70.9d; 810.8 keV gamma); Co-60 (Ni-60 + n → Co-60 + p; or Fe-58 + n + n → Co-60 + p; t½=5.27yr; 1173.2 + 1332.5 keV gammas; most important long-term ACP); Mn-54 (Fe-54 activation; t½=312d; 835 keV); Cr-51 (Cr-50; t½=27.7d; 320 keV); Fe-59 (t½=44.5d; 1099+1292 keV); ACPs dominate occupational dose in PWR maintenance; modern BWR: HWC (hydrogen water chemistry) reduces Co-60 deposition ~10×
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl: activated corrosion products are not primary Chernobyl hazard (dwarfed by fission products); but relevant for: ongoing decontamination of Chernobyl Units 1-3 primary circuits (Co-60 remains active; major dose source for decommissioning workers); ISF-2 fuel assemblies: Co-60 in cladding activation = why cladding must be maintained intact; NSC radiation field: Co-58 fully decayed (0.1% remains after 99.4% decay from 2026); Co-60: ~36% remains at 2026 (40yr/5.27yr = 7.6 half-lives; 2⁻⁷·⁶ = 0.37%—actually 0.6% remains: 0.5^7.6); see reactor_activation_products_REAL.csv
source: Clegg 1995 Water Chemistry Nuclear Power Plants; reactor_activation_products_REAL.csv; chernobyl_decommissioning_physics_REAL.csv; radiation_shielding_engineering_REAL.csv

details: RBMK coolant chemistry targets: pH 6.8-7.2 (near neutral); control: ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH) addition; hydrazine (N₂H₄) for O₂ scavenging: N₂H₄ + O₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O (thermal decomposition above 200°C; decomposes to NH₃ + N₂); demineralized water (conductivity <0.2 µS/cm); dissolved O₂ <50 ppb; Fe <20 ppb; PWR Li-7 chemistry: LiOH for pH 6.9-7.4 (soluble boron pHstat); Li-7 target: avoid Li-6 activation (Li-6 + n → H-3 + He-4); tritium production from Li-6 negligible at low Li; CANDU heavy water (D₂O): separate chemistry (lower moderator activation); RBMK advantage: no need for boric acid dilution changes (all control via solid rods + operator adjustments)
chernobyl_application: pH chemistry impact on Chernobyl cleanup: cleanup water introduced into reactor building (Akimov pumped cooling water throughout April 26 night) → highly contaminated water (containing dissolved fission products) flowed to basement = eventually became contaminated water flooding of basement; 5000+ tonnes water removed from basement; contaminated water management = major cleanup task; Cs-137 in water: soluble (CsOH); easily removed by ion exchange; Sr-90: more complex chemistry; ion exchange removed >99% from cooling circuit water; groundwater contamination: pH of CEZ groundwater (pH 6-8) = favorable for Cs-137 fixation to FES clay but Sr-90 remains mobile at near-neutral pH
source: Robertson 1994 Water Chemistry Nuclear Power Plants; chernobyl_groundwater_contamination_REAL.csv; chernobyl_environmental_remediation_REAL.csv

details: RBMK steam-water drums (SWD / барабан-сепаратор): 2 per loop; purpose: separate steam from two-phase coolant exiting fuel channels; design: cylindrical pressure vessel; centrifugal separators inside; dry steam exits to turbine; liquid water recirculates; SWD operating conditions: 7 MPa; 284°C saturation temperature; steam quality at drum inlet: ~14-19%; steam delivery: 1400 kg/s per loop (total 2800 kg/s to turbine); RBMK unique feature: each channel has individual feedwater flow control valve; allows individual channel power/flow management; compared to BWR: similar concept (direct cycle; steam to turbine) but BWR uses single pressure vessel; RBMK individual channels = multiple failure points but also isolation capability; turbine driven by: steam produced from reactor heat (Rankine cycle; see nuclear_fuel_cycle_burnup_REAL.csv)
chernobyl_application: Turbine rundown test April 25-26 1986: electrical blackout scenario test; turbine coast-down maintains cooling pumps for ~60-75s until diesel generators start; test REQUIRED: reduction to 700-1000 MW(th) (low power); xenon pit reduced power to 200 MW(th) (0.8% rated); at 200 MW(th): safety systems: low steam pressure → automatic ECCS trip signal; operators disabled ECCS trips; at 200 MW(th) steam quality low → SWD steam space partially voided → additional reactivity; starting turbine coast-down at 200 MW(th) with disabled ECCS + ORM=8 = conditions that triggered accident; steam drum pressure instruments: at 01:23:40 (AZ-5 pressed): SWD pressure begins rising → positive feedback already underway; reactor power had already begun uncontrolled rise before AZ-5

details: Primary circuit radioactive inventory during normal RBMK operation: N-16: ~10¹⁴ Bq (dominant; clears in 3 minutes shutdown); Kr/Xe from fuel pin failures: ~10⁹-10¹² Bq (dissolved in coolant; escapes via SWD vent system); Tritium (H-3): ~10¹¹ Bq (production from Li-6 trace + B-10 + ternary fission; t½=12.3yr; collected in vent system); I-131 from fuel pin failures: ~10⁸-10¹⁰ Bq (controlled via ion exchange resins); Cs-137 from fuel pin failures: ~10⁶-10⁸ Bq (controlled via ion exchange); reactor water cleanup system (RWCS): continuously processes 1% of primary coolant flow through ion exchange; RBMK: primary circuit chemistry monitoring: fuel failure detection via cover gas monitoring (Kr/Xe rise → fuel pin failure → operator action); RBMK allowed operating with failed fuel pins (unlike PWR which typically shuts down within days)
chernobyl_application: Shutdown vs accident: normal shutdown → N-16 clears; inventory dominated by short-lived Xe/Kr then by fuel-pin leak activity; after Chernobyl accident: ALL coolant/fission product inventory released instantly via steam explosion + graphite fire; estimated 5-60 EBq activity released to atmosphere in first hours (noble gases instantaneous); Cs/I in primary circuit water: ~4 EBq → released via open core; the comparison: normal operating primary circuit activity ~10¹⁴-10¹⁵ Bq vs accident release ~5×10¹⁸ Bq = factor 10,000 above normal in-circuit inventory (because accident released FUEL inventory not just coolant inventory)
source: Bell 1973 ORNL-5150 radiological analysis; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; 01_source_term_REAL.csv; source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv
